title: SMSF tied to Part IVA breach
full_text:
An SMSF trustee who was successful in overturning a disqualification for breaching the sole purpose test, providing financial assistance to members and failing to give effect to their investment strategy has been unsuccessful in proving a Part IVA issue was not present in regards to the sale of shares from a trust to his fund.
The case, Commissioner of Taxation v Merchant; Merchant v Commissioner of Taxation [2026] HCA 39, concerned a long-running matter regarding the actions of Gordon Merchant and the sale of Billabong shares from the Merchant Family Trust (MFT) to the Gordon Merchant Superannuation Fund (GMSF).
The acquisition created a capital loss for the unit trust that was offset against a capital gain, with the ATO deeming the transaction was executed for this tax advantage and not for the benefit of the SMSF and its members and thus breached the sole purpose test.
Those actions resulted in Merchant being disqualified by the ATO from being an SMSF trustee, but this was overturned by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, which noted Merchant had acted on advice and the risk of future non-compliance was highly unlikely.
The Part IVA matters were pursued in separate legal actions that were heard by the Federal Court, full court of the Federal Court and then the High Court during March this year, with the ruling handed down on 4 November.
In that ruling, the High Court held Part IVA of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 applied to the trust’s sale of the listed shares to GMSF, which was a related-party SMSF, and unanimously held the dominant purpose of that transaction was to obtain a tax benefit through the realisation of a capital loss.
In making its ruling, the court noted there was documented tax advice that recommended GMSF acquire the shares “with the result that the trust would crystallise a significant capital loss”.
However, buying the shares was inconsistent with the SMSF’s investment strategy and the $5.8 million MFT received was less than half the $12.8 million tax benefit postulated by the full Federal Court.
Additionally, Merchant, as trustee of GMSF, “did not want to sell, and would not have sold, the shares to unrelated third parties”, but as a result of the transaction they stayed within his group with no change in the ultimate economic owner and no divestment of investment risk.
author: Jason Spits
